utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: This was a few days after you were heard by a parliamentary commission in France.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We have the entire question missing from line 22, or, rather, at least part of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it exact to say that on the 24th of February, that was a few days after you were heard by a parliamentary commission in France?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My answer is this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to read this newspaper article before?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I read it the day following its publication.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I'll read the last paragraph for the transcript, and then I will ask a question of you. "General de Lapresle, former commander of UNPROFOR, expresses a feeling already expressed by his piers. He suggested that the Bosnian President, Alija Izetbegovic, had abandoned the enclave maybe on the basis of an agreement with the Americans. What a pity, once again, that the deputies of this mission were not more pugnacious and precise in their questions." When you were working for the OTP, did you interview General Lapresle?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you testified in 2001 before the parliamentary commission in France -- this is Exhibit 5D15; page 16 in the French version, page 12 in English -- page 16 in the French version.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm interested in Mr. Ruez's answer. We were just there a minute ago. Just further down. Yes. This is the paragraph in the middle, and the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You stated this: "We did not ask France for any information. Therefore, I cannot assess the quality of the cooperation we would have received from France." You, therefore, never called on the help of the French Secret Service during your investigation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: But General Janvier, wasn't he holding an important position at the time of the fall of Srebrenica in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was the commander of the UN protection force based in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: In the course of your investigation, did you speak to General Janvier?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Madam Fauveau. I hate to interrupt you, but he premises his answer on a very important statement, stating that he was not the right person to answer the question as to what sort of cooperation from various governments had been forthcoming. He mentions that he was just a member of the Office of the Prosecutor and is not part of the structural tiers of the President of this Tribunal. And he told President Rene Andre that the right person to be addressed on these matters ought to be the Prosecutor. Yes. Please go ahead. So, in other words, the fact that he may not have interviewed, I don't know who, doesn't mean that he may not have been interviewed by others.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I may clarify this with the witness. Indeed, I believe that his answer had to do with two different things.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: When you said that the right person to answer this question put by Mr. Andre would be the Prosecutor, you probably had in mind the cooperation of France with the Tribunal, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question I'm answering is on a previous paragraph, because the president of the commission says that I did not ask -- I did not answer on a question related to the collaboration of various governments, and to that -- to that collaboration of various governments with the OTP, my answer was that I was not a good person to be asked about this and that that question would have to be addressed to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And, indeed, the part I was interested in was whether you contacted the French Secret Service, and you said you didn't.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that the OTP has an audio recording of an intercept from the Zvornik Brigade on the 17th of July, 1995, and that in this earlier recording you can hear French?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Were you able to understand what was said in French in that recording?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. It assumes facts not in evidence. There is, in fact, no French spoken on that recording, so that question is not a proper one. If she can reword it, it shouldn't be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The point to the previous question made by the witness -- made by Madam Fauveau is whether he is aware that the OTP has an audio recording of an intercept from the Zvornik Brigade on the 17th of July, and that in this earlier recording - that's how we have it in English - "earlier recording," you can hear French. And the witness said: "Yes, I am." So very rightly Madam Fauveau is assuming that he is also familiar with the content of this intercept, or at least in the recording. So I see no problem at least. I stand to be corrected if Judge Kwon -- but I see no problem with her following up with her next question, because she rightly assumes that he's familiar. If you're not familiar with this tape and you only know of its existence, then you tell us so, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the question -- there's not a proper foundation for the question. If the question was, "Did you hear -- is there a conversation in French?" That question has not been asked. I think the questions will -- I will sit down, because you'll see the answer. I don't want to give you the answer, but you'll see why that question needs to be asked as a proper foundational question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I know exactly what you mean, but -- yes, Madam Fauveau, go ahead. Or at least the witness can -- because he was interrupted before he started answering the question. Can you answer the question that was put to you by Madam Fauveau, and after, of course, having heard Mr. McCloskey as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The answer was yes, I am aware that some French can be heard on one tape in possession of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And have you gone through this tape or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I was told that it could be overheard, French speaking, on this tape but not any content of what was said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And in spite of all this showing, proving the presence of -- a French presence in the zone in 1995, you did not ask for the help of the French Secret Service?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What's your objection now, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again foundation. I don't think it's intentional, but this is misleading without the proper foundation. The fact is the intercept says -- a Muslim intercept operator says "French can be heard being spoken in the background." That's all there is. There's no audio. There's no writing in French. And so if that can be made clear, this is a fine line of questioning. But that needs to be established by foundational questions before we go further, in my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the matter can be handled without any problems by the witness who ultimately has already confirmed that he never listened to the tape. I mean, your question would assume that, having listened to the tape, he should have found good reason why he should have involved, or at least got involved, the French security services. But if he had not listened to the tape, how -- where is the logic in the whole -- the whole -- there was French presence. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry, just to clear up factually, there is no audiotape of this. This is one of those handwritten note intercepts that merely states, as far as I can remember, "French is heard being spoken in the background," and that will help make these questions make more sense, I think, if we start from that foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. You obviously have much more information than I have -- or, rather, I don't have any information at all. But yes, Mr. Ruez, can you handle this question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Fauveau is interested to know why you did not feel the need to engage the services, or at least involve the French security services.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because, as I said at one point during my testimony, we make a difference between witnesses and sources. In the course of this investigation, we had various sources, including intelligence personnel working for IFOR, then SFOR, and most of the intelligence collected in these circumstances are not later embedded in the result of the investigation, because we know we will never present some witnesses in a courtroom. This was, in fact, the situation for this event. Having learned about this handwritten note, I made contacts at Sarajevo to learn a bit more about this situation, and unofficially I could learn that indeed, probably July 14 or 15, a few elements of UNPROFOR intelligence went to Zvornik in order to inquire about the refugees, I mean the missing part of the refugees. As far as I know, but I never formally interviewed anyone about this, these intelligence folks were swiftly directed from the Zvornik Brigade towards Bratunac. Due to the dates, that makes sense. 14, 15, they were not at the best place as far as the Bosnian Serb army could see the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Apart from this, but you haven't answered the other part of -- the basic part of Madam Fauveau's question, namely having gone through all this, why didn't you feel the necessity, the need to refer to the French security services?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reason is that there was no special reason to believe that, in connection with the events that followed the fall of the Srebrenica enclave, the French had any specific information related to that, since the main area of focus for the French at that time, as General Janvier and others have already said it, was the situation in Sarajevo. The situation in Srebrenica at that time was not really a concern for UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just to clear this up. Would it have been regular and possible for you to contact directly, as an investigator, to contact directly sources in the French security services? Or would you have had to refer that first to your superiors who would have done it for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would absolutely have to be done through the Prosecutor, through the OTP, in an official.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And to wind this up: Did you ever ask the Office of the Prosecutor to contact the French security services in connection with this intercept or what -- in connection with the findings that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not about this intercept. And more generally, I would not have done it because there was absolutely no lead to suppose that the French had any specific information about that place at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think, unless this matter has been exhausted and you would like to go deeper into it, please pass on to your next question, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one further question in connection with this topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did the OTP at any time inquire into the part played by the French Secret Service in the fall of Srebrenica? Do you have any information to that effect?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard some amazing pieces of propaganda during the years working on this investigation. I, indeed, heard some fantasy in connection with the fact that the massacres had been committed by French special forces in order to shame the honour of the Serbs and prepare an aggressive bombing campaign on Kosovo. I don't know if you refer to such articles or statements. But, no, we never investigated these statements and these allegations.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, you are a French official, a civil servant. Did the French authorities ask you to protect the interest of France in the course of your investigation?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said when I was talking about my links with the French authorities during the six years I served at the Tribunal, I said that the only connection I had with the French administration was the fact that I was every six months paying my civil pension in France. Aside that, I went on the 14th of July to the annual party at the embassy when I was not on mission. I participated at two official dinners at the embassy. And I never had any connection with any of the French ministries during these six years spent at the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You had your microphone switched off, so you need to just confirm that you told me that you don't have any further questions on this subject matter and that you're moving to the next topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to show the witness Exhibit 5D20. This is a document which I see has been translated into English. But, first of all, I would like the first page to be shown in B/C/S to the witness. Can we scroll down the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because we owe this to the public who is following. I'm informed that we do not have yet an English translation of this document because it has not been provided to us. So please do attend to ...

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm told that the translation into English was put in our electronic system last Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Someone check on that. I don't think it is there. Thank you. It's not yet in the system, so let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I shall continue using the B/C/S version, the Serbo-Croatian version, and I shall read what is on the first page of the B/C/S version so that you understand what we're talking about. "Pursuant to the order from the commander of the Joint Command of the army of the Federation, SP, number 7-1/07-203-2, dated 16 February 1998, and in response to the request from the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY from The Hague, please find herewith the reports collected RI and the organisation and establishment structure of the Drina Corps of the army of Republika Srpska." Is this a page which the Bosnian authority handed over to you in 1998?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could we now move on to page 2 of this same document. On the top left-hand side of the document, we can see: "Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Army of the Federation of the Bosnia and Herzegovina, VJ 5022, number 03/2-3/598, Tuzla, the 3rd of March, 1998." And to the right-hand side, we can see: "Military secret, strictly confidential." In the middle we can read: "Establishment formation of the Drina Corps." So is this a document that comes from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we now look at page 5 of this document. You can see a list of names here. Is it right to say that all these names end in "ch"?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And "ch" was sometimes used in Bosnian documents to replace "c" with an accent on the top.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably because --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I don't think the answer has been recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I heard him say -- probably because of the typing, but we don't have the entire -- can you repeat your answer, please, Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On the comment that it is typed "ch" instead of a "c" with a diacritic, my assumption is that this is due to the fact that the machine that was used maybe didn't have that diacritic. But I'm waiting for the point of Ms. Fauveau, anyhow, of the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: The question was as follows: I wanted you to confirm that in some Bosnian documents you saw things spelled with a "ch" instead of a "c" with a diacritic sign on top.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never noticed that specifically before you raised the issue, but yes, indeed, we can see here it is written "ch" on the names.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you have no reason to question the authenticity of this document; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And anyhow, the structure of the Drina Corps received by 2nd Corps was not supposed, in our eyes, to be an accurate document, since it was the compilation of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him finish -- let him finish, Madam Fauveau, because this is what is creating this confusion. Go ahead and finish your answer, Mr. Ruez, please. Let me read out to you what we have here. Answer: "A. No. And anyhow, the structure of the Drina Corps received by 2nd Corps was not supposed, in our eyes, to be an accurate document, since it was a compilation of the --" and there we stop.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of the intelligence collected by 2nd Corps about the Drina Corps. This document -- I mean, this structure had been requested in order to start what we call the military analysis that was a topic -- the subject of study of our military analyst Richard Butler. So it was designed then to be crossed with additional documents. So to answer the question of Madam Fauveau: No, we had no reason to question the authenticity of this document because it was provided to us by those who had collected this intelligence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One answer, maybe. You seem to be familiar with all this lettering and typewriter, et cetera. If you look to -- at the right-hand columns on those documents, you will notice that the -- now it's all capital letters. On the left it's -- except for the titles, it's small caps. On the right it's capitals. And there, "Mitrovic" doesn't end with "ich," "Milanovic" doesn't end with "ich," and no other name that appears ends with "ich." Do you an explanation of that, since you seemed to explain the previous -- what you said previously on the basis of maybe the typewriter not having --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have really no idea about this. As I said, I discover this issue of "ch" and with or without diacritic, but I still don't know what Madam Fauveau wants to ask me about this, at the final stage. I have no expertise on this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will see that on the right corner the "c" at the end of Covic, Lakic, Mitrovic, there is a "c" with an accent there. What kind of accent, I don't know what kind of accent that is because I can't see it very clearly. If you were to transport that "c" to the left against any one of those names, would it be enough to eliminate the need to use the "h" as well, or would it be a different "c" over there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Listen, I'm really not an expert in that language, but I can see that on Slavko Peric -- no, it's not on this one. There is another one where it has two branches on the "c". I have no idea about the habits of the person who typed this document. I really don't know what to tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Anyway, your witness. He's back to you, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Just to clarify. What I'm interested in in this document is that this is, in effect, a document which belongs to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Bosnian authorities, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, as it was provided to the OTP by the 2nd Corps of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: That was the sole thing I was interested in as far as this document is concerned. You said on the 15th of September, page 41 of the transcript, as follows: [In English] "I am among the first one who would expect more truth to come out of these trials." [Interpretation] I would now like to know whether you feel that the whole -- that the whole truth has not been said about -- has not been established about Srebrenica yet.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, because they are still -- there is still the potential for new information. This investigation is very broad, is hitting a large number of crime scenes. Each of these crime scenes could be a topic of an investigation in itself. We know from previous experience that, indeed, trials can add truth to this investigation process. The guilty pleas of two defendants is a very good example of that. And I am -- I also have the belief that until all the persons are indicted, and I'm thinking mainly about General Mladic, won't face their Judges, we won't have a chance to indeed have the full truth on these events, since some people who still could have the opportunity to express themselves, General Tolimir, President Karadzic, never decided to come and face the Judges. They have preferred so far to let their entire officer staff to be accountable for their own actions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You worked for a long time for the criminal investigation department of the police department in France, and you worked a number of years for the OTP here in the ICTY. So you were in contact with -- have you ever -- with legal affairs. Have you ever heard about legal errors being committed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't answer the question. Please rephrase your question and be specific. At least it may be a matter of interpretation, but what we have here, "So you were in contact here with," and then we have a blank. "Have you ever -- with legal affairs." Again, there is a blank. "Have you heard about legal errors being committed?" Where? By whom? I mean, he has to be put in a position to know what question he's supposed to answer. As it is, I mean, I wouldn't be able to answer any question of that sort. So please repeat your question or rephrase it in a manner which would put the witness in a position to answer it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You have worked for various legal institutions, international, national and domestic institutions. Have you ever heard of a miscarriage of justice?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to answer that question, Mr. Ruez? Because I think we have all heard of miscarriages of justice, so it's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- it's in every statute book which -- both when it comes to substantive and procedural rights of accused in every country. Yes, Mr. McCloskey, do you want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection on those grounds, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Same objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: His master's voice. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it right to say that the quality of the investigation largely depends on the resources provided to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only, but indeed resources are a very important element to an investigation, not only for the success of an investigation but mainly for the comfort in which an investigation can or cannot be conducted in the long run.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Am I right to say that you did not have enough resources available?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I make no secret about that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On the 14th of September, 2006, sir, you said that you had received all the reports provided by the UN soldiers but also the reports that had been sent to their respective ministers of defence. And more specifically, the transcript of the 14th of September, page 16 to 32, you stated as follows: [In English] "And then it was a more lengthy process with the Dutch military. It took some longer time, but the requests were fulfilled when they were launched." [Interpretation] Is it right to say that the OTP received the DutchBat reports?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the OTP received all the reports from the Dutch soldiers, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And among these DutchBat reports, there were DutchBat reports that had been sent to the north-east sector of the UNPROFOR mission in Tuzla; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Did this include the reports which DutchBat sent to the Dutch Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no recollection of, let's say, the various origins of material that we got from the Dutch Ministry of Defence. But what I meant was that the process was lengthy because of the way we were organised in order to conduct that process. So it was a bit a stop-and-go situation that lasted for a while. And also to say that once the requests were forwarded to the Dutch authorities, we received what we were asking for. So if we asked for this document you're talking about or this source of documents, yes, if we asked, we received.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, who would know whether you did ask to receive these documents?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would need to check into our archives among all the requests that were made to Dutch authorities, and we would see everything what we have requested.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Madam Fauveau. Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. General Gvero would not like to put any questions and dulce imfundo. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think I can finish before the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, good afternoon, Mr. Ruez. I have very few questions for you, and I hope I can keep them short and you can keep your answers short. One thing I don't think you -- I believe you've told us is the first occasion on which you visited the town of Srebrenica itself. When was that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time entering Srebrenica town was April, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You've been asked some questions, both in chief and by Madam Fauveau, about the mosque in Srebrenica town. That wasn't, in fact, the only place of worship in the town, was it?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was a total of five mosques in Srebrenica in 1992. My check was only on the obvious situation of the two mosques. But we did not push the situation to check all the mosques of the town. And I don't know if there was any other place for worship than these mosques, other than the Orthodox church in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. There was an Orthodox church there as well, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you ever visit the Orthodox church?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Since the building was standing, there was no ground for further checks in this town. We were not doing tourism, if this is what you mean, to visit the inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you come into possession of videotape footage of the interior of the Orthodox church and the state it was in prior to July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You've never seen a videotape showing the interior of the Orthodox church prior to 1995?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never seen any.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you ever come into information that indicated to you that prior to July, 1995, the interior of the Orthodox church had been desecrated?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had heard that the information that the Serbs in the area had was that this Orthodox church had been destroyed during the siege of the enclave. The only thing we could observe is that the church was standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But your evidence is, is it, that you've never seen video footage or never been told what the inside of the church was like prior to July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we move on very, very briefly, please, to the Kravica warehouse. You said this morning to Madam Fauveau that many of the sites that you visited and inspected were, as it were, sites that were part of a war zone and accordingly had damage that was attributable to fighting in the area.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Does that equally apply to the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could also apply to the Kravica warehouse, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I mean, for example, without going through all the photographs that you took, we see a lot of damage to the exterior of that building, don't we?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you would say, would you, that the damage to the exterior of that building was all caused by bullets?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And some of those bullet holes are 4 or 5 metres off the ground?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: High.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm not going to take that point any further. I'd like now just to show you a few of the images that were part of your presentation, and I'll give the 65 ter numbers and, for the benefit of my operative, the numbers in the presentation. Firstly, please, can we have 65 ter number 1724, and that's image 231. I'm not going to ask you any questions about how these images came into your possession but I want to establish with you that, so far as you're concerned, that photograph or those two photographs establish that the primary grave site at Orahovac was disturbed sometime between the 7th and the 27th of September, 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can we move on to 1723. That's the next photograph. It's image 232. And that's a similar photograph of Orahovac. Moving on to 233, please, the Petkovci dam. Again, two photographs which you would say showed disturbance of the primary grave site at Petkovci sometime between the 7th and the 27th of September; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just two more. 234, disturbed earth at Kozluk. Again, the same two dates, the 7th of September and the 27th of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. One moment. I hate to do this, but my attention is being drawn that, although we can follow you a hundred per cent because we're seeing these pictures roll on our screen, Madam Registrar is telling me that these would not correspond with the photos that were, indeed, shown by the Prosecution. I don't know exactly what the problem is, but there seems to be a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's very easy for me to deal with that and I will do. I can give the 65 ter number of every photograph, I can give the number that it is on the disk that was disclosed to us, and I can correspond it to the disk that Mr. Ruez used, which is slightly differently numbered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you think so. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to be clear, it's not a question of the image because it's the same images. It's the numbers we're talking about and the numbers were -- one of the things that is clear is the numbers that were used in court are very clear and that's what we should be using.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But which number would you -- for example, I'm looking at 234 at the present moment. Forget that it says 234 of 262. In reality, I take it it would be 234 of 271 or 272.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It should be 243 of 271.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why would it change? Why would it change? Because I would imagine that the only change that would occur is between 263 and 271.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No. No. Mr. Ruez added some images to his presentation with a subsequent disk and he produced a composite disk, and the numbers, I think, go in somewhere around 180, 190.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but we need to know. Because what we're looking at, and I take it everyone else is, I can't say what the witness is looking at. But what I'm looking at in sequence was 232, 233, and 234 of 262.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Those were the three aerial images that we saw in sequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, what was used in court when he first testified was 243. So if Mr. Haynes could keep with that segment, I think that should get us back on track.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It may be simply cured if I simply say: I'm going to show Mr. Ruez on this disk images 231 to 235, which, on his disk, are images 240 to 244.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think we can proceed along those lines, if it's not too confusing for you, Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You can see the photograph, at the end of the day, Mr. Ruez, can't you? I think lastly can we look at 235, which is 244 on your disk. And this is dated the 27th of September. On this image there have been some squares drawn to show what appears to be actual activity on that date. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, do you also agree that the sites that we have seen in those aerial images are all the primary grave sites in the Zvornik municipality?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For those that you have just shown, this is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You do agree with that, that we have just seen all the primary grave sites in the Zvornik municipality.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And, according to the aerial images that you have seen, all of the primary grave sites in the Zvornik municipality were disturbed in a 20-day period in September of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that's a maximum period. It could have been less than that, of course, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we contrast that, please, by going to photograph 238, which is 247 on your disk, 65 ter number 1610. Now, this is a primary gave site at Glogova in the Bratunac area, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And, quite separately and distinctly, we see that this is being disturbed towards the end of October, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all I want to ask you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have 25-minute break now. Is there going to be re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: A few questions. Let me look at my notes. It shouldn't be very long, I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How long do you reckon?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No longer than 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then we need to have break. I will not keep everyone here. So it's another 15 to 20 minutes and then you can go. A 25-minute break. Thank you. I am told Mr. Nicholls has a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I was just wondering if there was anticipated to be Judges' questions or if I should make the next witness available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, there are not going to be any Judges' questions, just re-examination by the Prosecution and that will be the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ruez, we are approaching and nearing the end. A few questions from Mr. McCloskey and that's it. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Hello again, Mr. Ruez. If I could give you something to take a look at. It's 65 ter number 1938. It's entitled "Bosnian Muslim Photo Identification Book". And I'm going back to the questions, if you recall them, by Mr. Ostojic when he was asking you about what effort you'd made to determine whether or not some of the Muslim men in Potocari may have survived. If you could just take a look at that book - you will know it's been a long time - and see if you remember that the -- I believe it was assembled, as you can see from the dates, during your tenure.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember very well this album.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the first part of it, to directly -- I've put a little yellow sticky. If you can go to that part that is entitled "Part 2 - Survivors," and I hope we can get it up on the -- I'm told we can get it up on the screen so everyone can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I notice Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to propose, to put it on the ELMO because our clients cannot see anything that Mr. Ruez is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's fair enough. And it's correct to say that this was an exhibit in the Obrenovic proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, it was, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it's something that counsel will tell you they've had for a long time. I passed out an actual physical copy to them, I think, a few weeks ago. All right. This is page 21. Well, page 21 is the page that's called "Part 2," entitled "Survivors". If you could get -- start with the title page, if you could, for "Survivors". There we go. Can everyone see that on the ELMO? So everyone can it on the ELMO -- I'm sorry, on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On e-court what we can see is a page which is "Part 2," those Bosnian Muslims identified as survivors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, does this help refresh your recollection on the topic I just mentioned and that Mr. Ostojic -- the same general topic that he was talking about?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And can you go to the next page so we can see what that is, and that will be -- we call this page 22. Okay. Can you tell us what this photograph reflects and why it was done for the investigation and/or trial?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a view of the -- the crowd in Potocari that was extracted from a video that was shown during this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what's the purpose of this? What's it trying to communicate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because Mr. Lazarevic had pointed out that for the benefit of the respective clients, it needed to be shown on the ELMO. On the ELMO -- I'm just checking. On the ELMO I can see nothing. But they can follow it on e-court. They all can now. Okay. I just want to make sure that you can all follow. Okay. Go ahead. I'm sorry. Yes, Mr. McCloskey. I just wanted to make sure that they follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you just give us a bit of a background? What was the investigation looking at when they looked this particular photo and all these faces, in terms of this document?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the photo it's clear that a certain number men can be seen. So these are the men who we believe were then separated before being able to get onboard of buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And the man with the number 1 on his shoulder there, it may be a little hard to see. It's down in the right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As can be seen on the document, this man was identified after my departure from the Tribunal --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we go up to the actual written product on the -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- since this was an identification done in September, 2002. But, indeed, we had started the process of identification of men that were visible on -- on the film, mainly the video, the V550 Zoran Petrovic film. We started that process in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can we go down again so we can see the photo and then go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I really don't want to interrupt my colleague, but I have some problem with this document that we have just seen. Obviously, it is said that it is taken from the Petrovic footage, and in my recollection I don't believe that this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this is not Petrovic footage. Petrovic footage is V550. This one has a different ERN number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I don't contest what you are saying, Mr. Ruez, but both in the previous photo, that's 22, on page 22, and this one on page 23, which you see, at the bottom of the page it says: "Petrovic Footage: Exact from video V000-3915." And the same applies to the previous one. If you look at the end you find exactly the same statement: "Location: Potocari, 12 July 1995. Petrovic footage: Extract from video V000-3915."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Some of these numbers tend to change with different versions of different videos. So I think this is a topic for cross-examination. I don't think that's really a problem, identifying which of the footage it came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is the ERN on both as well, anyway, if that may be helpful. But thank you for your observation, Mr. Lazarevic, and your remark, Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next page, and if we can have it so we can see the information, the investigative information, on it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, this is another man that, according to the investigation, was identified as alive after this photo was taken; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was also done after my departure, but indeed I learned about the fact that this man was alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you recall this video being shot in Potocari at the time?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you have any explanation why these men in this video -- well, there's a couple more like it, so before I ask that question let's just flip through them quickly. If we could go to the next page. Is this the same video section from Potocari as you know it?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So another man that has survived; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next one. Is this the same area in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And another man that has survived?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's see if there's any more. The next shot may be -- okay, that's the -- let's go to the next shot, then, the next picture. Okay. This is another man that has been identified as surviving?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At a different location, and I don't think this one -- I mean -- no, March, 2000. Sorry. I have no specific recollection about this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Well, let me go back to the question I was at. The men that were clustered in that area, Potocari, do you have any explanation how it was that they all survived?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only speculations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, do you have a conclusion based on the evidence that you can share with us?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Object to the form of the question, Your Honour. The witness clearly "Only speculations" and now counsel is insisting to get an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, this area was brought up by Defence counsel, and I'm not sure "speculations" in the way Mr. Ruez is always referring to means the kind of speculations we're talking about. And I think it would be helpful for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Provided he doesn't speculate. I mean, because he's just -- when you asked him, all right, let's go back, "do you have any explanation how it was that they all survived?" He said, "Only speculations." So at that point in time, if he can only give you speculations, how can you proceed with the next question, "Well, do you have a conclusion based on evidence that you can share with us?" It would still be a speculation on his part, even if it's based on some kind of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, you may very well agree that his answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Rephrase your question. Why do you maintain, Mr. Ruez, that if you tried to answer Mr. McCloskey's previous question you would be providing -- you can only answer it by speculating? Is there no evidence that you can rely upon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reason why I say "speculations" is that I would have no hard evidence to support the reason why I think these men are alive. But I have no evidence that supports my personal conclusion on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does that mean that there is evidence, but in your mind it would not be conclusive and would only allow you space to speculate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be speculation, because I interviewed no one on the Bosnian Serb side who told me what the reason was. So I can only imagine what the reason was, and it's an obvious reason to everyone. These men have been filmed by a Bosnian Serb camera, so it would not be a very wise thing to separate these men and get rid of them. That's the only explanation. So speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it is still speculation in your mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, you're aware of the -- do you know what date, whether it be the 12th or the 13th, that that group in Potocari were filmed?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it is the V550, Zoran Petrovic, it would be 13 July. If it is the camera crew that was together with General Mladic, and I think this is the case here, then it's July 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's the second -- the second case, as you thought. Now, if it is, in fact, July 12th, is it in -- can you tell at what time of day or at what point in the process of moving out the population this is occurring at all, if you can?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is at the very beginning of the process. The process starts after General Mladic has finished to address the crowd. We know from a certain number of witnesses that at the beginning of the deportation men could get onboard of buses, but then the system was getting tougher and tougher until no one could any more get on board of -- no men could get onboard of a bus before being separated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that last information you gave us, was that based on the evidence in the investigation or was that pure speculation?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- that was coming from the interviews conducted with the refugees who managed to reach Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I think, Your Honours, just for brevity we don't need to go through the rest of the book. We'll have another witness that will talk about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You certainly need to look into this question of the source of these photos, because if it's -- if what the witness has repeated now, namely that if it's the 12th of July, then it's not the Petrovic video but it's the other one, I think you have to revise the presentation of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely. That's another good reason to put this off, because I think the witness is correct on that. So we'll look into that. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, you mentioned that there was a list of some -- I believe roughly 200 Muslims, men that were taken by the Dutch, Muslim men that were in Potocari; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know if those names were compared to the missing list from the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was compared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you have a recollection generally of the results of that comparison?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is that they were all missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go to one statement made by Ahmo Hasic. Now, this is a comment that -- from the Krstic trial that he mentioned in answer to a question: "They took us to buses and to Bratunac, the old school, the one that had been vacated. At the time, I didn't know what its name was, but the name of the school is Vuk Karadzic, the old hero." Do you recall that Mr. Hasic has made this kind of a -- this statement to you or your investigators as he did in the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that. Again, if Hasic Ahmo is the survivor of Branjevo farm, the old school, it's the Vuk Karadzic school complex but it's the so-called technical school, not the Vuk Karadzic school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He is the old person that we've been referring to, as I think has been part of the record. As far as your investigation is concerned, has he always been consistent about where -- what school he was at, aside from this problem of whether it's the complex or the school?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what location is that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me, the old school, the one we call the old school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's the one identified as the old school on the photographs?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, you had mentioned that you did not investigate the events prior to the fall, but you did mention Mr. Butler and his review of these matters. As far as you know, did Mr. Butler review documents and intercepts that occurred prior to the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not be able to say today. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I thank you for that, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Ruez, we don't have questions ourselves. Mr. Ostojic, what's your problem now?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's not a problem at all. I would just like to clarify two points that were just raised in redirect, if permitted, based on a document that was not shown to a witness during his direct but initially introduce now in his redirect. So they're very short and no more than four or five questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, provided it's brief, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, good afternoon again. With respect to this 65 ter number 1938 that you have in front you now, I thought Mr. McCloskey's question that I have written down, on page 71, line 14 through 15, was: "What effort you'd made to determine whether or not some of the Muslim men in Potocari survived." We see in that photo album, if I can call it that, that those were efforts that were made well after you had departed the Tribunal, such as the dates showing 2002; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That's a misstatement of the evidence which will confound the issue. There are some dates. They go both ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I understand that if my learned colleague wants to testify and share that in argument with the Court. I'm limiting it to the pictures that he's seen. I don't want to go beyond that unless the Court wishes or permits me to do it. He's asked him, and I think he answered quite candidly, although I shouldn't be testifying, that: "These were not my efforts," these were efforts of someone else but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I still can't follow what you're asking. For example, let's take the first photo. That is the one shown on page 22. You have a photo. One man is identified there with the number 1. Identification is explained later on. And it's presumably -- this is what is of -- "identified by himself during an interview with local authorities in Tuzla as communicated to OTP by BiH on 19th September 2002. See annex 7." Now, if you see the other one, again, as communicated -- it doesn't say when the interview with Kada Omerovic was held, and it's communicated on 19th September. The next one is the same, and the next one is the same, and I think we can stop there. But what's your problem? I mean, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The problem, it's a subtle issue. I thought Mr. McCloskey's question, on page 71, lines 14 through 15, asked this witness quite pointedly: "What efforts you've made to determine the survivors." It's obvious even from his answer that he says that this was done in 2002; he had left already. So -- well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But he can still answer the question as to whether he himself -- I mean, when he was put -- when that question was put to him, he had not yet seen these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: He had seen the entire file, Your Honour, and he said: "What efforts have you made? Are these the product of your efforts?" I think, with all due respect to the witness and my learned colleague, it is misleading. And I want to know from this witness if the question is what efforts he's made, that he's made those efforts, presumably, during the time that he worked at the Office of the Prosecution as the lead investigator. But let's make it short, in the interests of time, and I just want to cover another point. If the Court believes it should be introduced, I'll accept that. I just have another question on another issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the questions by my learned colleague regarding the Dutch list. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I would still be willing to answer very briefly the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's okay. No.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You asked it so you have an interest in the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. It's whatever the Court would like.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's going to be very short. This identification process of individuals that can be seen on film started as soon as we had access to these pictures. It was run through the assistance of the police in Tuzla. And then the effort that was made was to take from people who knew the persons who are identified, to take from them a statement that we named "Last Time Seen Alive," so that we will be sure of the fate of that person before being on that picture. This process continued during the years, and in fact, yes, was restarted sometime later. And let's say the first five pictures of this book are the only pictures where identifications were made after my departure, though the request for some of them was done during my time of presence here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now, directing your attention to the question relating to the Dutch list. Do you remember that? Basically it just happened.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me from whom you received this Dutch list?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, the Dutch list, we received it through the intervention of someone whose name is Ivan Lupus, who later worked at the Tribunal but who at that time was working at the Human Rights Committee of Helsinki, and who investigated this specific point during the summer 1995, because we had to time to deal with that. And indeed the list showed up, after having been discovered more or less at random, in Zagreb at the UN headquarters. It was then sent, I think, to the Ministry of Defence of the Netherlands, and from there transferred to Foreign Affairs who provided it to the OTP. That's my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on your investigation and the interviews that you've done with the DutchBat personnel, who made the list specifically from the DutchBat personnel?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a hundred per cent sure of the name of the person. I think it was Major Franken, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think you might be right. Are you aware, based on your investigation, that Major Franken has previously testified and given a statement that the Dutch list was lost? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was what we were told initially in 1995, but it was apparently not lost for long because we ended up getting it. But, yes, it started out being lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When did you get it?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would think before the end of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's all I have. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think that brings us to the end of your testimony, Mr. Ruez. Of course, I barely need to remind you that unfortunately you will be recalled at a later stage when we have clarified the matter that was raised last Friday relating to the aerial images supplied by the US government. As soon as that is dealt with in a definitive manner, then you will be recalled back. Of course, there will be arrangements made with you which would enable you to consult your superiors to fix the date. I wish to take this opportunity to thank you on behalf of the Trial Chamber, also on behalf of the Tribunal, for having been kind enough to come and give evidence in this case. Of course, you will receive all the assistance you require to return to Paris. And on behalf of everyone here, we wish you a safe journey back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will stay on call for any need of this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please don't go to your island in the Caribbean again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, may the Office of the Prosecutor be allowed to talk with Mr. Ruez in the meantime? I don't -- about just logistics, normal things, not about aerial -- well, I don't know. I don't see any real problem talking about anything, but I would -- I know what the normal rules are, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's easily dealt with and in the normal manner. You're not to discuss with Mr. Ruez anything which relates to his possible future evidence on the aerial images. As regards other matters, provided they are not going to be the subject matter of further testimony by him, you can, of course. But I make it clear that there are no dealings in relation to his future -- what could be his future testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the understanding is when he is recalled, he is recalled only for the purpose of being cross-examined on the aerial images and not on other matters. I'm making this clear to the Defence teams as well. All right? I thank you so much, Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My pleasure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So I think we can start with the preliminaries. Yes. Let's deal with the exhibits first before we bring in the witness. Mr. McCloskey, which exhibits do you wish to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, basically the -- I believe it's 272 photographs which came under the number P02103, along with the various video shorts that came in with his evidence. And I can give those to you now. They have 65 ter numbers, and the first one is -- these are all Mr. Ruez's personal -- more personal to him than the general, as you recall, trial video. 1514 is south to Srebrenica town; 1545, Srebrenica to Potocari; 1557, Potocari to Bratunac; 1590, Kamenica to Sandici; 1575, Kravica warehouse; 1686, Nova Kasaba graves; 1701, Grabovci school; 1718, Orahovac; 1759, Kozluk; 1796, Branjevo farm; 1820, Pilica cultural dome or centre; 1870, the exhumation of Cancari 12. Now, what I have left out of that is the segment that we call the trial video, which was that big compilation. There's one more segment to that which we chose not to play. It's basically DutchBat at the Hotel Fontana, which you will soon see. So I think after -- after you see that section, we will be moving that into evidence. And if counsel's going to have any objections to anything particular, please let me know so that we can prepare for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So any objections for the admission of -- yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. This is about Exhibit 02103, which was the difficulty in following the evidence of this witness. I think that the most blatant difficulty we have with exhibits thus marked is the photograph that Mr. Haynes wanted to show to the witness. We had three types of identification. That was the 65 ter number. Then numbers from 1 -- from 231 to 235, that was the material that was disclosed to the Defence on the 24th of August. And the numbers 240 to 244, which is contained in the list delivered to us by the OTP where we have the numbers from the 65 ter list. The objection of the Defence is as follows: We don't wish to obstruct in any way the evidence of this witness on this basis, but what will be the problem - and I believe that Judge Kwon already noticed this - when we come to examining the evidence and to drafting our briefs, there will be certain exhibits that we will have difficulty in referring to. Our proposal is as follows: All the photographs that cannot be matched or are not equal to the numbering used by the Prosecutor pursuant to 65 ter, that those exhibits be assigned new 65 ter numbers so that we could, in our future proceedings, refer to them by those numbers. So this refers only to Exhibit P2103. We don't have any other objections concerning the other exhibits. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think -- I don't know. I want to hear you first, Mr. McCloskey, but I think that would make it much more confused than it actually looks now, because my understanding is that 2103 is what we were seeing on the screen throughout the testimony of Mr. Ruez when it had the full 271 pictures. In other words, they may not correspond with what Mr. Ruez himself had, but I don't think we should worry about that. What we should worry about is what we have in 2103, as it was rolling on the screen as we went by during his testimony. If I am not mistaken. In which case, I think it is better to have 2103 as it is, but, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with you, Mr. President. But the problem with 65 ter numbers is not a problem at this stage. I think the evidence, as it came in, was clear and I don't think that's the problem that -- that occurred here. The problem that occurred here is that we did not provide 65 ter numbers for everything, because I assumed that they were all pretty much the same. That won't happen again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We will provide 65 ter numbers for everything. But there's one legal issue here that I think we could address that -- because, as you know, I've gotten in the habit of arguing with Mr. Bourgon but he's not here and I know he would love to argue this issue. I believe his argument was that he was looking to 65 ter as an exclusionary rule, that if it's not on the 65 ter list, it should be excluded. Now, we have searched for any precedent to that and we have not found any. We did find a case out of a trial chamber in ICTR called Prosecutor versus Simba, where this same argument came up and the court said, no -- just because it's not on the 65 ter list is not a reason to exclude it, that you must go back to a balancing test and determine whether or not there has been prejudice and whether there has been notice. I think we understand that the reason for 65 ter is to provide both parties with proper notice so they're not surprised. But if we're going to actually get into the admissibility of this evidence, we have to go down to 89(C) and (D). And this is the balancing test. Based on Ms. Nikolic's argument, I think that that's no real surprise by any of these photos. It's the problem was we didn't -- we didn't have numbers for the slightly different photos. So that would be my position, and I think the Defence will probably share that because they will have a turn, and I'm sure not all of their numbers will -- all their exhibits will have 65 ter numbers. Things come up. As we saw, I had asked Mr. Ruez, because one witness mentioned that there was a brick wall at Orahovac and I knew a photograph that would solve that problem, so I asked Mr. Ruez to show us that photograph. Very similar to a 65 ter number, but it did not -- did not have one. But I think it helped everyone. That will come up with the Defence. And I think you yourself have said there is some flexibility. So I think if we go to 89(C) and (D), that's where we -- I'm sure we might have some good arguments in the future with counsel, but that's where we should be, not in 65 ter. And I will not let this 65 ter issue that I know Judge Kwon and others are concerned about happen again. We will get ourselves more up-to-date and do what we have been doing. When we find new material, we have been filing motions to get it on the 65 ter list. We've done that before; we've done that after. We will continue to do that and alert everyone that when we have documents or items that are not part of that process, we'll get them to them as soon as possible so that we can have an 89(C) and (D) argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will come to this again tomorrow, because we have to stop. I would, however, like to -- and we'll finalise the tendering. Madam Usher, please, if you could kindly bring in the witness so I can explain to him why he has been kept waiting for these 45 minutes. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I know it's late, but I just wanted to inform the Chamber of the fact that we have encountered a problem as far as the upcoming witnesses are concerned. The DutchBat documents exist and they are in the hands of the Prosecution. As far as we know, we have never seen them, and I think it's most important that we read these documents before the DutchBat witness starts his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Please, we are not going to discuss this now. You will deal with it as soon as we finish. I'm sure Mr. McCloskey will cooperate with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning -- or good afternoon to you, sir. Please make yourself comfortable. I'm not going to keep you here long. I just wanted to explain to you why you have been kept waiting in a room and not been escorted here to start your testimony. The answer is that we had some further questions to put to the previous witness. It was anticipated that they would last from 5 to 10 minutes. Unfortunately, there were legal issues that arose at the same time, and the whole process took the whole 45 minutes. So please accept our apologies for this. You will come again tomorrow morning. We will resume with your testimony -- or we will start with your testimony. That is all I wanted to tell you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So we'll start tomorrow morning at 9.00. In the meantime, try to thrash this amongst you, and we will first conclude the tendering. Of course, there are documents to be tendered by you as well. Thanks. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 19th day of September, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.50 p.m.,
